> ​@SofiaHerege I think I understand what you are trying to say, and for me there is no contradiction between your points on capitalism and what I previously wrote. With a bit of nuance.  
>   
> Let's see:  
>   
> 1. There are many definitions of socialism, and many branches thereof. But on a fundamental level socialism is a behavior of groups of people and a particular leaning in a style of government that strives to gain an equal quality of life for its individual members by enforcing an equal distribution of rights and resources (value).   
>   
> 2. Socialism - or rather a "high measure" thereof - occurs naturally and works best in tiny groups of people, where it is prudent and often necessary to lean heavily into equalizing individual outcomes in order to ensure survival of the entire group; yet it ceases to work on the scale of thousands, let alone millions or billions of people, where it disproportionately a) requires heavier enforcement b) reduces productivity of the society, as it focuses on re-distributing value instead of creating it, c) destabilizes society.   
>   
> 3. Capitalism, at its core, is a transactional model and by extension a leaning in a style of government, in which the creation of common wealth is facilitated by creation of individual wealth - added value; hence, the right to own (private property) and private capital, in conjunction with market evaluation. The core principle of capitalism is that you need to create value for other people (for the market) in order to gain individual value.   
>   
> 4. In real life there is no 'pure' socialism, just as there is no 'pure' capitalism, but a varying measure of each in a current political and social milieu. Capitalism and socialism are not mutually exclusive. In fact, since the beginning of the 20th century many countries adopted novel mixed forms of government, and have been shifting across the spectrum with a varying degree of success.  
>   
> 5. Both socialism and capitalism as societal frameworks in their limit will always lean to a pyramidal, hierarchical structure, which is invariant to human societies on a large scale. A capitalistic monopoly is a form or variant of such pyramid. That's why 'too much of capitalism' (e.g. kids working in mines & factories 16h/day, or a single person having as much wealth as almost everyone else combined) can be as bad for the majority and the society as a whole as too much of anything. Nowadays, there's a problem with the excesses, I suppose.  
>   
> 6. Capitalism leans towards monopolies, and they are most efficient, but only to a certain extent and over a period of time. In other words, they are most efficient until they are not, when a monopoly breaks down, and a new monopoly is gradually formed, etc. The giants crumble under their own weight due to inefficiency and unsustainability, only to give way to other giants forming. But in the process and all around new, smaller players can enter the market's competition. As well as create new markets altogether. This is akin to the elite theory: no one clique sits on the throne for eternity; a rotation in one shape or form always occurs.   
>   
> 7. In the 20th and 21st centuries socialism as an elastic model of government became a tool used by political entities to gain power and keep it in their hands, using the promise of a better life for certain sub-groups of the society at the expense of others; hence the electorate minorities: workers, peasants, beggars, women, ethnics, invalids, sexual deviants, migrants, etc. Which at its core is a D&C tactic. People aren't equal and shouldn't be too equalized by force. It 'unites' people and divides them at the same time, creating the modern globalism - a mixed government model that levels the vast majority of the population (socialism) and concentrates most of the value as well as means of producing it in the hands of the few who govern (capitalism).  
>

### **@PHExpatPrepper** | 👍 598 likes
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E83dpuyvpiM&lc=Ugy2IzbnIdfw3xumKKx4AaABAg)

I worked 17 years at a large US based semi conductor, survived 4 rounds of "redeployment", yet noticed each time the 'older' folks seemed to get the brunt of it.  Regardless of work performance.  Then I would see rounds of new hires come in later (young and cheap).  Me and my wife (a Filipina) started to put together an exit strategy.  We stopped spending, downsized, and saved.  At 45 we pulled the trigger, sold all US based assets and moved to the Philippines. We took our savings, built a commercial property and bought an older home to live in.  Created two business that today still thrive.  We have ZERO debt, and after a few years of being frugal, we then bought a new car (cash saved up).  Now at 57.. and seeing the struggle so many around the world are having, I am so very happy we did this.  Being a prepper is not just about rice and beans.

Always great when these videos drop.  I rarely comment on YT but I am led to say what Professor Jiang calls weakness, things like moderation, environmentalism, immigration and soft power…could, in fact, be Canada’s greatest strengths in a volatile, multipolar world.

For me, I think Canada isn’t trying to out-America America, and frankly, it doesn’t need to do so. It’s got to play a different game.

The danger also is to see power through a 20th-century lens: military might, empire, domination…Canada doesn’t need that. Instead its focus should be on quietly building a post-industrial model, one that prioritizes stability, trust, equity and long-term resilience.

And on the environmental front? Maybe I am biased, but we need to stop seeing sustainability as a burden. It’s a strategic advantage for society. Clean tech, green energy and responsible resource development are the future, and Canada is well-positioned to lead.

As for immigration, let’s be honest, every country is having to deal with it, even the poorest and most fragile. The question isn’t how to stop it. It's how to turn it into an advantage. Canada could do this by attracting young, skilled, motivated people and giving them the chance to contribute. Smart immigration can mean smart nation-building.

You don’t have to shout to be the strongest. Sometimes, those countries that don’t make the most noise are the ones actually preparing for what comes next.

I think the problem of canada specifically is something you briefly mentioned, the lack of civil ambition of canadian socioopolitical cultural and national identity, and the accumulation of not only economic but also social wealth and not doing anything with it. Canada has produced too few intellectual capitals on the foreign market, the canadians who do produce this capital usually go to other nations projects or entities for better pay or opportunity. 

Perhaps the American empire is to blame for that, Canada is basically a vassal state. We export and import much of our social capital. If intellectual and social capital was encouraged to remain in Canada, both the US and Canada would benefit more greatly than the current trend of this social capital exporting itself for better opportunities, leaving Canada itself abandoned and at greater risk for discohesion and instability from the American point of view. 

Another issue is that for some reason Canada has been late to developing the necessary infrastructure of resource production; two fold issue: Canada has too thin of federalization across all its provinces and needs to strengthen the federal capacity to create and maintain nation-wide infrastructure across provinces, and the provinces themselves having either developed no oversight or arbitrary oversight that hasnt been made for national utilization of these resources. 

Relating to the previous is Canadian politics both in the regard of demographics and bureaucracy; part of this is the FPTP which unfortunately has allowed for probably the least productive 20 years in recent Canadian political history and also the demographics both of the MP and provincial electoral are such that the political environment does not promote ambition or ingenuity.

I think these are maybe peripheral symptoms of what you are identifying as the boomer problem. I think you're right the only thing we can do is be truthful to ourselves and history, about the world we've made and where we find ourselves in it. The west needs a difficult discussion with itself.

### **@marcoaureliomorgado4794** | 👍 2 likes

Hello, Professor Jiang! My name is Marco Aurélio, and I am a Physics and Natural Sciences teacher on the island of São Vicente, off the coast of the state of São Paulo, in Brazil. I am a "baby boomer" (I am 62 years old), I am divorced, and I have no children. My father owned a grocery store and is now 87 years old and can barely walk. He depends on my sisters and me for adequate healthcare. Despite my age, due to successive changes in retirement laws in Brazil (there have been 4 in less than 20 years), it will still take me about 5 years to retire (if I am still alive or if, at least, I have a minimum of health to do daily tasks for myself).
I agree when you say that baby boomers are selfish. However, like any large population group in this capitalist West, a minority are rich or at least have sufficient resources to access the best doctors, diagnostic technology, and hospitals where resources are not lacking. Most people (elderly or not) depend on the public health system, which is large but precarious in many places. Therefore, the average life expectancy of "baby boomers" in Brazil depends on social class and prosperity: the vast majority will die before the age of 75, while social classes that earn around $25,000 a year or more (after all taxes, fees, and labor charges have been deducted) will live on average around 85 years of age. I earn less than $20,000 a year and cannot afford a good health plan because, in addition to being expensive, the monthly price increases with age. I have no one to take care of me if I get sick.

What I mean is that most baby boomers will die due to lack of medical care, because they live in places where urban infrastructure is deficient, and because they have no one to take care of them. And this is not only the reality of Brazil, but of the vast majority of the "Global South". In other words, if, on the one hand, the world elite are "baby boomers," on the other hand, the vast majority of the world's baby boomers are dying in painful agony.
My mother died of Alzheimer's disease at age 80. I am terrified of the possibility of having the same disease or some other neurodegenerative disease. If that happens, I will not be a burden to anyone: I will commit suicide.

My husband and I are baby boomer that born in early 60s, migrated to Canada in 1990s. We are working classes, making humble incomes, have children, and enjoyed the peaceful and beautiful environments here. Both my husband and I are lucky baby boomers that born and raised in Hong Kong and Macau. Both places have no political issues and comparatively advanced in education, economy and healthcare. My parents came to Canada with most of their children. Therefore, I have a very smooth transition with my parents and siblings all living in the same places. I have retired and my children have grown up and working. This is the first time in my life feeling the stress of the society economically and politically. New graduates are hard to find jobs, and the realty markets are turning bad. I hope Canada can keep its old days but the world is changing. Yes, I still wanted my healthcare and pensions as it’s hard to depend on my children. Life is not hard but it’s never easy to save much for the working classes. I have enjoyed my life, and if we are the ones that needed to go so that our next generation can live better, we’re willing to let go. I never agreed upon speculating on housing markets, this is not healthy for the growth of our society and for the generation to come. I had been believing many of us in our generation shared the same values, that we wanted our children to have better life than ours. Maybe, when one got the power and money, people changed.

“It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.” I’m a baby boomer, that is, someone who was born after WW2 between 1946 to 1964 in a time of economic prosperity. Half of our generation are not wealthy as you would have your audience believe. We worked hard and lived a good life. Most of us were what you could call, “the Middle Class.” Half of my generation are struggling to help their children get into a house. So it pains me to see you explain that the state we find ourselves in is blamed on Baby Boomers. You are wrong sir.

I have watched most of your videos and am impressed with your lectures that shed light on history, consciousness, philosophies, and secret societies to explain how the world works, in Broad, General, Terms, interlaced with some Speculation. I am a first generation Canadian of European descent, my parents were liberated by Canadian soldiers. There was nothing wrong with our national identity and we were proud of this country and our place in the world. I hardly recognize my country anymore, the changes have been seismic. Let me list a few:

1. Working class families that relied on a single income. Moms stayed home to raise 2 or 3 kids. This meant safer neighborhoods, we walked to school and played outside. We had only one car, and one black and white TV, one rotary phone mounted on the wall.

2. Our family doctor made house calls. Milk came in glass bottles delivered to your home, as was your mail, and newspapers. Gas stations had service attendants that pumped your gas, checked your tire pressure and washed your windshield. Many gas stations also had 1 or 2 bay mechanical repair services. We had “corner stores” typically run by Chinese immigrants where the owners lived in the back and sold soda pop, candies, cigarettes, chips, milk, eggs, and a few other household groceries. Small business was alive and well. Shoe stores, cafes, photographers, salons, music stores, TV and electronic stores, everywhere. No malls, no super stores. Families ate dinner together every night. Many of us did simple auto repairs, skills we learned in high schools with wood working, machine, and automotive shops.

We used to be a full service, self reliant, entrepreneurial society of small businesses with a thriving Middle Class. Jobs were abundant. The future looked bright.

In all of your lectures you have failed to note the pace of progress, the avarice of capitalism, the stealthy creep of monopolies, technological advances, the rise of corporations and their influence on government. And now, where are these services? The small businesses? The jobs? The Middle Class? 

How naive and convenient it is for you to blame the Boomers with your sloppy theories professor, you have missed the mark.

### **@AlixPrappas**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E83dpuyvpiM&lc=UgxFJjNYi0HrTe5AB8h4AaABAg)

Firstly, I'd like to thank you for your contribution of your analysis of modern geopolitics.  The synthesis is compelling and appears true in many ways.  

With that said, your causal explanation of the decline of the west appears reductionistic.  You suggest that it is the Baby Boomers who are the "real" cause of the decline.  You assert that it is not the immigrants, or the Jews, or Trump, or Putin but US because we have become selfish, lazy, and corrupt.  Amen, I agree with that emphatically TO A LARGE DEGREE. However and once more, this is overly reductionistic, not differentiating between levels of causality and culpability.

Did Roman decadence and corruption cause the fall of the Western Roman Empire or was it foreign invaders? or was it economic destabilization? 

The truth is that it was the confluence of all of these factors and more.  The corruption was the catalyst that allowed for the second-order causes to proliferate.

The same is true today regarding the fall of the West.  We are principally to blame, our corruption.  However, the Jews and immigrants and many others also bear responsibility.  It is wise to give evidential weight to the magnitude of the contribution of each factor of the decline, of which, our corruption is primary.  It is not helpful, however, to flatten causal influence.

Took out loans to finish my degree.  Shopped resale and discount stores for most things.  Spent lots of my paycheck for supplies for my classroom.  Finally able to buy a small house on the very lowest end of the market.  My grandparents lost everything in the Great Depression.  My father served in WWII, and struggled afterwards.  Four kids… mom sewed our clothes, we all helped out with chores and yard work.  Took a few vacations camping.  Never received lavish gifts… made sure to stay out of debt.  My father died of cancer at 49.  So, no, don’t paint baby boomers with a broad brush.  I’m not selfish, I didn’t suck up all the resources.  I have savings.  I’m trying to make sure I have enough for my old age.  Single income.  Live off my monthly income.
